newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine unions, gov't try to break labor deadlock.
newsitem.headline: Argentine unions, gov't try to break labor deadlock.

text.p: Argentine trade unions and the Peronist government, locking horns over President Carlos Menem's attempts to reform labor legislation, resumed dialogue Thursday to try to reach an agreement on employment policy.

Menem's Cabinet Chief Jorge Rodriguez, flanked by Labor Ministero Armando Caro Figueroa and Interior Minister Carlos Corach, went to the headquarters of the CGT labor federation to try to mend fences after December 26's 24-hour strike.

GT chief Rodolfo Daer, his negotiating position boosted by court rulings that Menem's attempts to reform labor laws by decree are unconstitutional, told reporters he hoped the talks would "result, God willing, in a great social pact."

But the unions, whose December strike was their third last year, appear unwilling to make concessions to the government's line that only the "flexibilization" of labor laws can help the country combat 17.3 percent unemployment.

Reducing joblessness is Menem's priority in a year where he faces tough mid-term Congressional elections in October. Some unionists are demanding that Menem dismiss Caro Figueroa for promoting reforms which according to CGT director Luis Barrionuevo "people interpret as slavery and wage cuts."

Daer urged the government to drop its appeal against labor judges' rulings that Menem's decrees, signed last month after talks with unions broke down, violate the constitution. Labor Judge Ines Gassibe annulled the decrees Monday on the grounds that they violate unions' constitutional right to take part in pay talks, deprived workers of acquired rights and go against norms of the International Labor Organization.

The decrees were aimed at loosening the union grip on pay talks by letting smaller firms bypass national unions in negotiations and letting firms appeal to the government if they want to negotiate with unions on a company-by-company and not an industry-wide basis.

Another CGT leader taking part in the talks, Juan Manuel Palacios, said consensus in Congress, even among the Peronist Party's own ranks, was against the decrees. But he believed they were a poor precedent for any social pact.
"Expectations are really not too good from my point of view, because the government attitude has shown clearly that it wants to continue imposing its rules of play," he said.

Daer wants the talks to include issues beside unemployment "such as the tax system, the state of regional economies and the situation of medium- and small-sized businesses." (( -- Buenos Aires Newsroom +541 318-0695))
